blocks.text: Africa’s venture ecosystem has grown rapidly: Partech Africa reports annual startup funding rising from under $300M in 2015 to $6.5B in 2022, of which $4.9B was equity and $1.55B debt (Partech Africa, January 2023), drawing global institutions, development finance institutions and sovereign funds alongside local managers. Research from the Africa Private Capital Association (AVCA), Partech, Africa: The Big Deal, FSD Africa and FinDev Canada has followed, much of it from the investor’s perspective: who deployed capital, where, at what valuations and with what returns.

The founder’s side is less systematically documented: not how much capital was raised, but how it was used strategically. When did founders raise, and when did they refuse? Which instruments did they choose, and why? Was the investor mix built around the best term sheet or long-term strategic relationships? Why stay lean through a devaluation rather than dilute to build a war chest?

This capstone examines how founders in nine companies made those choices. Because capital strategy is contextual, the aim is not a formula but a sharper shared vocabulary for financing decisions, and a set of documented examples, for founders and investors alike.
The founder’s side is less systematically documented: not how much capital was raised, but how it was used strategically.

blocks.html:
Research question
How have some of Africa’s most successful founders used capital as a strategic tool throughout their growth journey, and what can founders and investors learn from their financing decisions?
Two sub-questions follow: how did each company’s financing choices relate to its business model and operating context; and which patterns recur across the cases, where do they break down, and what conditions explain the difference?

blocks.text: Success is defined by observable indicators. A company is treated as a scaled case if it meets at least two of the following:

items: demonstrable scale (a consistent, disclosed revenue base);
geographic expansion beyond the home market;
a documented exit or partial liquidity event.

blocks.text: Five companies meet this test: M-KOPA, MNT-Halan, NALA, Moniepoint and LemFi. Autogirl, Feegor and Earthbond do not yet meet it on disclosed evidence (Autogirl has expanded into Ghana, but its revenue scale is not public); they are included as early-stage cases for the way they designed their capital needs, not as proven successes. Sendy, which closed in 2023, is the cautionary case: a company that attracted institutional capital and expanded across markets before failing. Moove’s 2026 exit from Nigeria is used as a comparator rather than a full case, because the seven dimensions were not applied to it.

The capstone profiles nine fintech and logistics companies across West, East and North Africa against a common framework. Section 2 sets out the method and its limits; Section 3 reviews the literature; Sections 4 and 5 present the cases; Section 6 compares them; Section 7 presents a capital-strategy framework for founders and investors; Section 8 sets out implications for investors; and Section 9 concludes.
